title: Building Collapse
description: Building collapses can occur due to structural failure, natural disasters, or accidents. Knowing how to respond if you are inside or near a collapsing building can save lives.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Building collapse is the catastrophic failure of a structure, causing it to fall or partially collapse. Collapses can result from structural defects, foundation problems, overloading, natural disasters like earthquakes or floods, explosions, or construction accidents. Building collapses can trap occupants under debris, cause severe injuries, and lead to loss of life. In India, building collapses have occurred due to unauthorized construction, poor quality materials, and lack of proper maintenance. Understanding building collapse safety and knowing how to respond is crucial for urban residents.

sections.heading: Warning Signs
sections.content: Learn to recognize warning signs of potential structural failure: deep cracks in walls or floors, doors or windows that no longer close properly, sagging ceilings or roofs, leaning walls, unusual sounds like creaking or popping, water stains indicating leaks, and separation of walls from ceilings or floors. If you notice these signs, evacuate the building immediately and report to authorities. Do not ignore these warning signs or assume they are minor issues. Regular building inspections can identify problems before they become critical.

sections.heading: During a Collapse Indoors
sections.content: If you feel the building shaking or hear sounds indicating collapse, drop to the ground immediately and take cover under a sturdy table or desk. Protect your head and neck with your arms. Stay away from windows, glass doors, and exterior walls. If possible, move to a load-bearing wall or interior corner. Do not use elevators during a collapse. If you are on an upper floor and cannot evacuate, stay away from the exterior walls and take shelter in the most interior part of the building. If you are trapped, protect your mouth and nose with cloth to avoid dust inhalation.

sections.heading: If You Are Trapped
sections.content: If you are trapped under debris, stay calm and conserve your energy. Do not shout continuously unless you hear rescuers nearby—shouting can cause dangerous dust inhalation. Tap on a pipe or wall rhythmically to alert rescuers. Use a whistle if available. If you have a phone, call emergency services if you have signal. Stay in a curled position to protect vital organs. If possible, use a cloth to filter dust from the air. Do not attempt to move heavy debris unless you are certain it will not cause further collapse. Wait for professional rescuers to reach you.

sections.heading: After a Collapse
sections.content: If you are outside during a collapse, move away from the building immediately to avoid falling debris. Do not re-enter the collapsed building until emergency responders declare it safe. Call emergency services (112) immediately and provide details about the collapse and any trapped people. Do not attempt to rescue others yourself unless you can do so without putting yourself in danger. Follow all instructions from emergency responders. Be aware of secondary collapses, which can occur after the initial failure. Help direct emergency vehicles to the scene if possible.

sections.heading: Safety Precautions
sections.content: Never ignore structural warning signs or evacuation orders. Do not occupy buildings that have been declared unsafe. Report structural problems to building authorities promptly. Ensure buildings are constructed following proper codes and regulations. Avoid unauthorized additions or modifications to buildings. Regular maintenance of buildings can prevent many collapses. During earthquakes or other disasters, follow Drop, Cover, and Hold On procedures. If you live in an older building, be especially alert for signs of structural problems. Support efforts for proper building inspections and enforcement of safety standards.
